name: Gentian violet

lead: Gentian violet (crystal violet) is a purple dye with antibacterial, antifungal and other properties. It has been applied to skin and mucous membranes for infections such as impetigo, ringworm, athlete's foot and thrush, which is its link to skin appearance: clearing an infection can clear the rash or lesions it causes.

It is also used as a skin marker before surgery or allergy testing and as a stain in laboratories. The WHO still lists it, though newer drugs have largely replaced it, and a 2020 dermatology review notes renewed interest in antiseptics as antibiotic resistance grows.

paras: Historically it is painted on the affected area as a dilute solution. It stains skin and clothing purple, and the colour can last weeks.

Rodent studies show carcinogenic and mutagenic effects, the US FDA says it is not shown safe for animal feed, and Health Canada in 2019 removed drugs containing it from the market and advised pregnant and breastfeeding women to avoid it. The dye is classed as causing serious eye damage and is suspected carcinogenic. It stains skin visibly.

angle.text: It is used to treat infections that cause visible skin changes. The dye itself stains the skin, so the cosmetic trade-off is temporary purple colouring.

lead: Gentian violet, also called crystal violet, is a triarylmethane dye with antibacterial, antifungal and anthelmintic activity.[1] It has been applied for fungal infections such as thrush, ringworm and athlete's foot, for impetigo, and in low-resource settings for burns, umbilical cord infections and mouth ulcers.[1]

For appearance, the relevance is as a topical anti-infective: skin conditions it treats cause visible rashes and lesions. It is also used as a marker ink on skin before surgery or allergy testing.[1] Its own effect is a purple stain that remains for days to weeks.[1]

Dermatology reviews describe it among topical antiseptics attracting renewed interest as alternatives to antibiotics because of resistance.[2] Safety has been contested: Health Canada's 2019 finding of carcinogenicity with direct body contact led to withdrawal of drugs containing it, while a 2009 letter in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology was titled 'Gentian violet is safe'.[1][3]

paras: Medical uses include fungal infections, impetigo, burn wounds, umbilical-cord care and oral candidiasis; the WHO still lists it though newer drugs have largely replaced it.[1] It is also used as a surgical skin marker, a laboratory stain, and an industrial dye.[1]

A mouse study showed dose-related carcinogenic effects at several sites, and the US National Toxicology Program reported carcinogenic and mutagenic findings in rodents.[1] Hazard labelling includes harmful if swallowed, serious eye damage and suspected carcinogenicity.[1] The dye stains skin for weeks.[1]

Methyl violet was first made in 1861 and crystal violet was synthesised by Alfred Kern in Basel in 1883. The name 'gentian violet' is thought to date to 1880, Hans Christian Gram used the stain in 1884, and Jakob Stilling described antiseptic properties in 1890.[1]

In 2019 Health Canada found gentian violet carcinogenic with direct body contact, removed drugs containing it from the market, allowed certain medical devices such as foam dressings for a six-month limit, and advised pregnant and breastfeeding women to avoid it. The US FDA issued a 2007 import alert on farm-raised seafood in part for unapproved antimicrobials including gentian violet.[1]

Trials include a study of topical gentian violet for cutaneous MRSA infection and nasal carriage[4] and a randomised comparison of one-percent gentian violet with one-percent clotrimazole for otomycosis.[5] A review of topical antibacterials in dermatology discusses it as a renewed-interest antiseptic.[2]
